of Hansard, and I open with a quotation from my question to the minister in this respect:
Will the minister tell us what is the expected extent of participation on the part of banks under the new scheme? Also will he tell us what is the anticipated augmentation from that source of mortgage funds, and how it may he expected that that augmentation will be made available for distribution in smaller communities?

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is difficult to answer those questions in detail. We do not know, for instance, to what extent the lending institutions will divert money they formerly put into conventional loans into the lending operations under the insurance mortgage technique. We would hope, however, that this would result in a great increase in the flow of mortgage money under the National Housing Act.
You will note, sir, that the minister, speaking, I take it, with reference to the existing approved lending institutions, is saying in effect: Well, we do not know whether they will be able to put any more money into their mortgage lending under the act. Then the minister proceeds:
With respect to the last part of the question, perhaps it can be answered more specifically than the other parts.
Then he goes on to deal with something to which I shall return later, but he does not answer my question as to what might be expected to be the over-all result of this legislation with respect to the supply of available mortgage funds. The minister was not prepared to estimate the amount of mortgage funds that might have been expected from the banks as a new source.
With that background let us look at these three aspects, and first of all the abolition of part I of the National Housing Act. Those of us who have tried to keep ourselves close to the housing problem will, I am sure, view the proposed departure of part I of the act with very great regret. Part I of the National Housing Act has been in force since 1944 and it has been, I think, as fruitful a piece of legislation as this parliament is likely to enact in the ordinary course of events. It has created an individual pool for each lending institution under which the government and the lending institutions have, in approved proportions, shared the risk. Seventy per cent of the lending for new one-family residential construction today comes from that source. In the first eleven months of 1953 we saw that joint lending under part I of the act provided for the construction of some 30,500 units. Conventional loans, on the other hand, as an investment for the funds of the approved lending institutions, attracted just $92 million by comparison in the same eleven months' period for 17,500 units.
The results, I think, are also to be measured in relation to the sound social

National Housing Act
purpose of encouraging the ownership by Canadians of their own homes. Let us look for a moment at the results that have been achieved in that period. The daily bulletin issued by the dominion bureau of statistics of March 17, 1953, had this to say about the trend of home ownership in Canada in the ten-year period up to 1951:
Home ownership made a big advance in Canada during the ten years from 1941 to 1951, according to a census bulletin on housing by tenure and type of dwelling published by the dominion bureau of statistics. Of the 3,409,295 occupied dwellings in Canada's ten provinces in 1951 2,236,955, or 65-6 per cent, were occupied by owners and the remaining 1,172,340, or 34-4 per cent, by tenants. This represents a substantial jump in both the number and percentage of owner-occupied dwellings over 1941.
Sir, for that jump, the greater part of which occurred in the seven-year period from 1944 to 1951 rather than in the three-year period from 1941 to 1944, part I of the National Housing Act deserves the bulk of the credit for the substantial increase there recorded in the proportion of owner-occupied homes in Canada. What of the period since 1951? In the daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics of January 8, 1954, we find the following:
Total number of households or occupied dwellings in Canada's ten provinces increased by 232,000, from 3,409,000 to 3,641,000 in the period of approximately twenty-seven months from the time of the 1951 census to September, last year, according to results of a special survey of housing characteristics and household equipment in private homes by the bureau.
Then it adds:
About 73 per cent of the increased number of dwellings was in single detached houses which rose by 172,000 to 2,448,000 units. Of the ten-province total, 2,451,000 or slightly over two-thirds were owned by the occupants.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I say that in accomplishing this result, so desirable both from the economic and social point of view, the provisions of part I of the National Housing Act are entitled to a measure of high praise. The government, of course, has participated and for the first eleven months of 1953 has earmarked approximately $106 million under the National Housing Act. In round figures there is $60 million for its share of the joint loans under part I of the act and $50 million on account of direct loans.
Let us remember again the credit that is due the approved lending institutions for putting up the other three-quarters of the total for all joint loans under these provisions. In the first eleven months of 1953 these approved lending institutions have accounted for an increase in new residential construction over the same period in 1952 of no less than 22 per cent. This is a tribute

both to the effectiveness of the provisions of part I and to the co-operation that has been enjoyed by the government from the approved lending institutions in administering these provisions.
In his statement on December 16 from which I quoted, the minister was wary in his comments as to what might be expected from the existing approved lending institutions in relation to the augmentation of existing sources of mortgage funds. From the same newspaper report of the statement issued on January 2 by Mr. George Holmes, president of the Canadian Life Insurance Officers' Association, I read this:
Commenting on the new housing legislation now before the House of Commons, Mr. Holmes said:
"It is too early to foresee the effect of the government's new insured mortgage legislation. The companies desire to co-operate with the federal government as they have done in past years to provide additional housing, but the volume of funds available for this purpose will depend to some extent on whether the interest return on the insured mortgages, having regard to safety and administration costs, is competitive with other avenues of investment."
I suppose we come back to this position, Mr. Speaker, that no one can say with certainty what will be the amount of mortgage money available under the new scheme.
I come now to the second aspect, the matter of admitting the banks to the category of approved lending institutions. In this respect the bill approves a fundamental departure from all Canadian banking practice and banking legislation of the past. The Canadian banking system is, as all members are aware, unique in the world. It has been a strong system. One has only to recall the strength exhibited by the Canadian banking system in the depression years as compared with the results in the United States, to recall gratefully the strength of the Canadian banking system. Unquestionably part of that strength has been due to the presence in the Bank Act of section 75, subsection 2 (c), which provides as follows:
Except as authorized by this act, the bank shall not either directly or indirectly
(c) Lend money or make advances upon the security, mortgage or hypothecation of any lands, tenements or immovable property . . .
To maintain the strength of the Canadian banking system, we must have regard to two features which I believe are of the highest importance, namely, security and liquidity. It is because there have been security and liquidity in our banking system and in the range of investments available to the banks that our banking system has been strong. The strength of the system also owes much to the quality of leadership we have had in the Canadian banks. Unquestionably we

have at the head of our banks some of the leading business executives and some of the most competent men in Canada.
The money in the banks belongs to the depositors. I am sure it will alarm not a few persons to learn that this far-reaching legislation was introduced, involving a fundamental departure from the principle of Canadian banking legislation as it has existed from confederation, without the banks being consulted by the government before the decision was taken and announced. Let us then understand that the banks have not asked for any widening of their powers in relation to investments of this kind.
Even if this legislation goes into effect quickly, it will still be necessary for the banks, in order to follow wise and prudent investment policies, to diversify their investments and to meet the traditional obligation of Canadian banks to finance the development of Canadian resources. Today bank funds are substantially employed. I do not believe the government is going to suggest there is any volume of idle funds in the vaults of the banks. It does not pay the banks to have idle funds. They make their profits from lending money prudently. On a recent occasion when the minister was speaking in the city of Toronto, he did hold out the hope that, without trespassing upon their existing volume of loans and investments for other purposes, the banks would have available a volume of funds arising from new deposits as the population increased. If the population increases, then certainly the demands upon the banks to finance increasing and expanding development of Canadian resources are likewise going to increase.
No one can fully answer this question, but in asking ourselves whether the banks are going to lend extensively under the provisions of this act let us face up to the fact that to find funds for its purpose the banks may be obliged either to sell government bonds, to call in existing loans or to expand credit. It is one thing, sir, to expand credit on commercial loans for a period, we will say, of nine months, but it is another thing to expand credit on mortgages having a lifetime of 25 or 30 years. In other words, it is an entirely new field so far as the banks are concerned.
If you will examine the December, 1953, issue of the statistical summary of the Bank of Canada, you will see that the 1953 gross national product at today's market prices is adjusted at $24,176 million. Out of that total Canada is devoting to housing a gross domestic investment of $1,032 million. That is a very high proportion going into investment in housing today.
National Housing Act
I say these things with a view to trying to put this measure in its true proportions before the house. It is so easy for people to draw the impression that because you are going to allow the banks to lend money on mortgage security, and that because the banks have billions of dollars in their balance sheets, suddenly you will have a gigantic infusion of new mortgage money available for mortgage investment.
Sir, it would be a bold man, one indulging in a good deal of speculation on the subject, who would be prepared to say with any degree of confidence exactly what amount the banks are prepared to devote to investment under this bill, by way of mortgages. I know we can assume that the banks will co-operate; but I hope we are not going to contemplate any pressures being exerted upon the Canadian banks to put depositors' money into long-term investments on mortgages under this act, when the course of bank experience and the necessities of preserving liquidity would dictate to those responsible for the banks' investments that they should not go too deeply into investments of this new kind.
Sir, the banks must continue to have regard to both liquidity and security in all their investments. Both are of the highest importance with them; but they are not the same thing. It may well be that the problem of preserving security with bank investments is going to be met substantially by the insurance provisions, under the scheme of this act. But let us recall, sir, that even though security is provided in that way, that in itself does not provide liquidity, because after all you can have a bank mortgage guaranteed against default, but if the mortgage goes on without default on the part of the mortgagor the bank's funds are tied up. And they are tied up for periods up to 30 years under the provisions of the new scheme.
Therefore the provision for insurance by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is no guarantee whatever of liquidity for these bank investments. What is proposed by the government in relation to liquidity, as the minister stated in his speech this afternoon, is that the Bank of Canada Act is to be amended to provide that the mortgage portfolio of chartered banks is to be eligible for loans from the Bank of Canada.
That will have to be considered a feature of high importance in assessing the provisions of this present bill in regard to the needed preservation of liquidity on the part of bank investments. I make only one further
1330	HOUSE OF
National Housing Act
comment on the matter of bank investment, and I do it by way of trying to bring this matter into its true proportions, and eliminating wishful thinking- which undoubtedly all of us have been tempted to do in this respect, not excluding the minister himself.
Speaking on the measure on December 16 last, as reported at page 1009 of Hansard, the minister made some comment in reply to a question of mine to which I referred earlier this afternoon-and I am now taking up the minister's answer at the point I broke off when reading earlier. I was asking him with respect to anticipated augmentation from banks of the available supply of mortgage funds. The minister's answer proceeded as follows:
With respect to the last part of the question, perhaps it can be answered more specifically than the other parts. I understand there are about 4,000 branches of the chartered banks in Canada. Each branch will now become a lending institution. That in itself will increase the number of lending agencies under the National Housing Act from some 150 odd, as there are at the present time-that is, branches of authorized lending institutions-to over 4,000.
I am afraid the minister has been indulging in wishful thinking in picturing every branch of the chartered banks in Canada as a local lending agency. It may be that the banks will in time use their branches extensively in relation to whatever mortgage business they choose to embark upon; but there has been no statement from the banks to that effect. And I just throw out a word of caution at this point.
To assume that the banks are going to pump vast resources into mortgage investments on the one hand, and also that 4,000 bank branches in Canada are all suddenly going to become local lending agencies, is to make an assumption that is not warranted by any authoritative knowledge that exists at the present time.
The third feature is this insurance scheme. This is designed, of course, to make the lending on the new terms palatable to the banks, and to encourage the present lending institutions to enlarge their mortgages. Because while previously approved lending institutions have been providing 60 per cent of the 80 per cent of approved lending value, from this point forward, on an increased lending value, they are expected to put up the full 100 per cent of the loan.
Let us remember this: all members in the house with legal training know that the law in relation to guarantees is a very technical branch of the law, and that it is necessary for a person who enjoys the benefit of a


guarantee to comply strictly with the letter of his contract, if he hopes to hold the guarantor to his guarantee.
While this insurance scheme has some precedent in the United States, our situation in Canada is rather different; and I do not think precedent in that respect can be pressed too far. Let us also recall that the loan is limited to 98 per cent of the mortgage risk. I am referring to the principal and the arrears up to six months. A 2 per cent premium is paid for it by the mortgagor. The limit of $125 may not be adequate to cover the expenses to the mortgagor; and for that reason I caution the house against assuming that the guarantee will be worth 98 per cent of the face value of the mortgage.
I make these further observations on this matter of guarantee. First, it is not open to individuals as mortgagors; it is confined to institutions. However, it will become open to individuals to purchase insured loans from approved lending institutions. Secondly-and this is a factor I ask the house to consider carefully-the limit of a loan which can be insured is a minimum of 70 per cent.
In other words, no approved lending institution which lends only 69 per cent of the approved lending value becomes eligible for insurance. It must be 70 per cent or more. I suppose that any of the approved lending institutions is prepared, under proper circumstances, to lend up to 60 per cent of approved lending value, without any form of guarantee or insurance. So we do not need to worry about loans up to 60 per cent of approved lending value.
But, sir, the effect of this bill will be that, in the case of loans in excess of 60 per cent and less than 69 per cent of the approved lending value, there is open to them no loan under existing practice from an approved lending institution on the one hand, and no insurance on the other hand. So that we should realize that in some cases at any rate we are insisting that the intending mortgagor, even if he can get along with 61 per cent of the approved lending value by way of loan, must take 70 per cent if the mortgage is to qualify for insurance.
The third feature that I should like to comment on is the necessity, the statutory requirement, that possession and title be given by the holder of the mortgage, the approved lending institution, to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in order to qualify for the payment under the guarantee. Is this such a simple matter that it can be just hustled over, Mr. Speaker, as has been done

by the minister today? Sir, this could be one of the major problems arising under the provisions of this bill.
It is a requirement of this bill that before the mortgagee can call upon the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to pay 98 per cent of the principal of the loan, plus the six months' arrears, the mortgagee first of all shall have obtained possession and title to the property in order to deliver title and possession to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. There is only one very slight exception to this rule in the bill. Sir, that means that the mortgagee must foreclose the mortgage. Indeed, under this bill, if a mortgagee permits the arrears of interest on the mortgage to accumulate beyond six months he is running the risk of losing the benefit of the guarantee with respect to any additional arrears. What does that mean? Well, I am quite sure that the mortgagees in this case are not going to risk forfeiting the benefit of the guarantee. They are going to be required to take such steps as will put them in a position to deliver possession to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. What does that mean? It means foreclosure. It means dispossession of the owner of the equity. There is no escape from that fact under the provisions of this bill, except one very slight saving provision which will be available under the bill in very few cases.
Anybody who has had any experience with the mortgage business, especially in the depression days, knows perfectly well that in the vast majority of cases the mortgagee does not wish to take over the property. He looks on his mortgage as an investment, not as an avenue by which he can obtain title to the property. In most cases he is not interested in becoming a property owner. He wants his money back, and therefore he will nurse the mortgagor, the owner of the equity, along as long as there is a chance of the owner of the equity making good.
Under this bill, sir, a holder of an insured mortgage dare not give additional time to a mortgagor, once his mortgage is in arrears six months, without jeopardizing his guarantee. Let the house, if it will, weigh that fact carefully. And if in time to come recession should occur, with a drop in real estate values, and the owners of equity are unable to maintain their payments, if that situation should arise then this bill would drive the holders of these mortgages to insist upon the letter of the law in their mortgages and to take steps in the event of six months' default to acquire title to the property and dispossess the owner of the equity.
National Housing Act
Now, sir, we are thinking about this in terms of what this legislation may contribute to sound social as well as economic purposes, the kind that parliament would approve. Is that a sound social objective? The owners of houses with insured loans upon them, in the light of this provision, are going to have a much more difficult lot than those whose properties are not subject to insured loans. It is going to demand of the holder of the mortgage that he insist upon prompt payment, and that he should not allow the mortgage to run into arrears, because he must be in a position to give possession to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Take this situation also, Mr. Speaker. We have had experience in this country in depressions of moratorium legislation being introduced by provincial legislatures. Suppose there should be a recession in this country. Suppose the recession should reach such a point that provincial legislatures again should decide to intervene as between mortgagors and mortgagees and impose a moratorium in such cases, preventing the mortgagee from qualifying to give possession to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in order to get the benefit of that corporation's guarantee. Here is the situation, surely, that the guarantee is intended to provide for when a mortgage goes into default. And yet in that case provincial legislation can prevent the mortgagee from obtaining possession of the property so as to put him in a position to call upon Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make good its guarantee, because he would not be in a position to give that corporation possession. That is not the only possibility, Mr. Speaker. Suppose some provinces, in the event of a recession, decided to enact debt adjustment legislation, decided somehow or other to intervene in this field for the purpose of adjusting debts. If legislation of any kind is introduced in this respect the beneficiary is going to be the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and a guarantee to that extent is going to be worth less than I am sure many hon. members now think or have been led to think it is worth.
I am not prepared to speculate today on the possibility of that recession coming. I do know that there are some very eminent people in this country who do say that they think there is evidence of the possibility of a recession. I notice that on October 14 last Mr. A. R. Mosher, the president of the Canadian Congress of Labour, was quoted in his speech at Vancouver as saying:
I do not want to be pessimistic, but I think there are some signs that a recession is coming.

National Housing Act That remark comes from a very prominent labour leader in this country.
I am not prepared to speculate on the question of a recession coming, but I do say that every hon. member must take into account the possibility. In addressing himself to this bill he must take account of the situation that would arise in the event of a recession occurring in this country, and a different situation arising from any that we have been facing in recent years.
Our housing legislation, you see, Mr. Speaker-and this goes for part I of the present act-has had the benefit, in those post-war years, of good times, rising real estate values and rare defaults on the part of mortgagors. What occasion has there been for any mortgagor to default on a mortgage, Mr. Speaker, when in most cases, unless he made a very improvident purchase, as the market rose he could sell for more than he paid? If that situation is ended, the factors that I have mentioned may come to be factors of high importance. In any event, I am quite sure they are going to be matters of importance for the approved lending institutions in weighing the value that they are prepared to attach to the guarantee provided under this bill and deciding to what extent they are prepared to reduce the return that they ask for the risks they take in connection with such loans.
There are two other matters that I should like to mention, Mr. Speaker. The first relates to the position and power of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under this bill. If this bill is enacted in its present form or anything approaching its present form, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will derive under its terms gigantic powers. Under the terms of this bill that corporation will become the sole arbiter of at least three things, each of which is of cardinal importance in connection with parliament's expectations from this bill.
First, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation becomes the sole arbiter under this bill of lending value. The bill provides: "lending value" means the value for lending purposes of the house or housing project determined by the corporation.
Indeed, not only must every mortgage under this bill, in order to be eligible for insurance, be approved by the corporation, but Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will itself make the appraisal. The minister told us this afternoon that the banks have not qualified staffs or personnel for that purpose. There is a very great power.
Second, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation with respect to every mortgage under this bill will be the sole arbiter of 
the standards and quality of construction. There are those who may take some satisfaction from the safeguards that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will insist upon in relation to standards of construction, but let no hon. member lose sight of the implications of the inescapable fact that under this bill Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation becomes the sole arbiter with respect to every loan made under the provisions of this bill for all Canada of the standards and quality of construction.
Third, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under this bill becomes the sole arbiter of the speed of construction with respect to every loan insured before construction is undertaken, because if the approved lending institution wants the benefit of insurance with respect to instalments made under a building loan it must accept the fact that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation controls the progress of construction. It must approve every single advance or instalment.
Speed is essential in holding down the cost of construction. In the report by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which I mentioned earlier attention was drawn to the fact that housing costs in Canada were stabilized last year only by reason of the fact that the average period of house construction, the average period it took for a house to be constructed from the time construction was started until it was finished, had dropped from 8 [DOT] 4 months in the first half of 1952 to 7-2 months in the first six months of 1953. Already builders in this country 'have indicated very serious apprehension about delays in construction with reference to provisions of this kind. I simply content myself at this time with drawing attention to it and seeking to impress upon the house that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under this bill becomes the sole arbiter of the speed of construction with respect to every loan approved before advances are made under it.
That is why I say that under this bill Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and its officials derive gigantic powers. Let us use the proper expression, whatever may be the implications read into it on occasions; it means the vesting of vast powers in a giant government bureaucracy.
One could use the illustration of the camel putting his head in the tent and working his way in by degrees. By this bill we see Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation growing from its modest participation originally assigned to it in the housing scheme and now stepping in and assuming the sweeping powers provided by this bill. For that reason builders are realizing how

vast are the powers the corporation will hold under this bill and are therefore taking a second look at the bill.
Before I leave that subject I desire to express just one further thought in relation to the possibility of defaults in the event of recession. When speaking on housing on April 28, 1953, the minister quite properly said, as reported on page 4491 of Hansard of that date:
I think it is important as a matter of policy that the federal government should neither be the landlord of too many Canadians nor should it hold the mortgages for too many Canadian homes.
That being the view of the government as expressed last April, let us remember that in the event of widespread defaults in the event of a continuing recession, if it makes good its guarantees the government will acquire possession and title to a great number of homes in Canada under this bill. Very quickly it will become the country's greatest landlord.
Next, the bill vests in the governor in council very sweeping powers to enact virtual legislation in the form of regulations. There are pages of provisions in the bill which vest in the government the powers to enact provisions in the form of regulations. This wide power to legislate by regulation could be applied, on the one hand, if the government so choose, virtually to nullify the legislation enacted by parliament. On the other hand, if used by the government for this purpose it could be made the occasion of rampant inflation in Canada. I express the hope that if this measure becomes law it will not be allowed to become bogged down under its own weight by reason of a multiplicity of troublesome regulations and that the government is not going to heap upon those who are going to have to work under it such a mass of paper work that it is going to make loans under its provisions distasteful to them.
The powers are so vast that those of us who do not trust power in the hands of the government will not feel that powers of this nature, powers which are so wide, so sweeping and so inclusive are needed.
The Bank of Canada is going to have an important part to play in the whole scheme, as was made apparent to us today. The liquidity of bank investments in this respect will depend upon action on the part of the Bank of Canada. Let us not lose sight of the fact that there is lurking danger of inflation here. This bill can go far beyond the present housing situation in Canada in its effect.
I have spent more time on this than I intended to in looking into the possibilities
National Housing Act
that could arise under this bill. As I say, in its effect it is going to extend far beyond the immediate situation. It is evident that in introducing a bill with powers as sweeping as this one the government is looking beyond the housing situation that exists. On the face of it, it looks as though the government is girding itself with another weapon to deal with the possibilities of recession, and is resorting to the Keynesian theory of economics.
It would appear as though the government was looking to this bill as a means of stimulating house construction, not simply with the view of improving the existing shortage but with the view of stimulating house construction in future as a source of labour and the encouragement of other consumer spending as well as having regard to the social effects which come from owner-occupied houses.
I apologize for the length of time I have spent in this review of the bill and its implications. 1 have done it because of the admittedly vast importance of the bill. It is extremely important that the opposition, in discussing a piece of legislation of this kind, should fulfil its duty to the house and to the Canadian people and give the most searching scrutiny to the bill so that if parliament chooses to adopt it and it should go into effect both parliament and the Canadian people will fully understand the possibilities that can arise under the terms of the bill.
It is government legislation. For that reason it will undoubtedly in due course be enacted by parliament. I have tried to point out today the fact that in the majority of its provisions this bill simply re-enacts the existing law. There are some of its other provisions which will help to mitigate our housing problem today. There are provisions in this bill which, if not wisely and prudently used, could be a source of danger to the Canadian economy. It is therefore necessary that both in this house and in the banking and commerce committee all hon. members should apply to this bill the closest and most diligent scrutiny.
When and if this bill becomes the law of this country, members of parliament should regard it as one of their highest duties to insist upon vigilant supervision over the administration of this measure and over the vast powers it confers upon the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the government. There must be searching study; there must be, it seems to me, an annual parliamentary review of all operations under this measure.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will And relief

National Housing Act
in recalling the fact that I have only forty minutes to devote to this bill and that I shall not be able to spend two. hours on it as did the preceding speaker.
This bill now before us is, as we are told on the title page, a bill that, when enacted, will become known as the National Housing Act (1954); and we are also told that it is an act to promote the construction of new housing, the repair and modernization of existing houses, and the improvement of housing and living conditions.
Notwithstanding the rosy picture painted for us by the minister when he introduced this bill, I am sure we are all satisfied that there is still ample room for improvement in housing and living conditions in Canada. Even the figures which the minister gave us, and which he summed up by saying we were making considerable progress, do not reveal the true picture of housing conditions in this country. I think the government is to be congratulated on the fact that in 1953 they completed 90,000 houses and started on around 100,000. I think they are also to be congratulated on the fact that at long last they have succeeded in completing in one year enough houses to keep pace with the newly created housing demand. This is about the first year since the housing act was put into effect, and I believe since the end of the war, that the government has in any one year succeeded in building more houses than the newly created demand in any one year.
The fact that from 1941 to 1951 we have reduced the number of persons per occupied dwelling from 4-5 to 4-1 does not convey the true picture as far as overcrowding is concerned. I shall point out later the extent to which I believe this bill fails to meet the need, and I shall have something to say in regard to that need.
This bill introduces certain new principles into the housing act and I presume it is hoped by the introduction of these new principles to solve the housing problem, at least to some extent. Among other things the government intends to terminate the system of joint lending, to insure loans that are made to assist in the financing of housing, and to bring the banks into the mortgage lending field.
The bill represents, I believe, a logical evolution of the present government's housing policy. The government apparently believes and persists in believing that private enterprise can meet our housing needs. The government is determined not to become landlord to any number of Canadians, at least not through the process of building homes fMr. Noseworthy.J
for them. It may, however, become landlord to a great many Canadians through the process of mortgage foreclosure. The government is reluctant to become a landlord and apparently is still reluctant to get very deep into the housing business. The government still believes that private enterprise can provide enough houses and provide them at a profit. Private enterprise will provide houses on no other terms. They believe that private enterprise can provide at a profit houses in sufficient numbers and at prices that will meet the housing needs of the Canadian people.
Every change that has been made in the National Housing Act over the years and the changes made in the regulations for the administration of that act have followed that general line of policy. I believe we have that policy carried almost to the nth degree in the bill now before us. Year after year the government has clung persistently to the idea that if we could only make terms with the lending institutions, if we could only grant them terms sufficiently attractive and they could be induced to put sufficient money into the mortgage pool, our housing problem could be solved.
Year after year we have had one concession after another by this government to these lending institutions in the effort to induce them to put sufficient mortgage money in that pool. Year after year every move made by the government in the matter of housing has given first consideration to the lending institutions while the basic need of the Canadian people for houses and the disastrous social effects of the housing shortage have received secondary consideration. Yet, notwithstanding all the concessions the government has made, the government has failed to induce the lending institutions to provide sufficient funds to make any appreciable reduction in the backlog of needed houses. The best that the government has been able to do is shown in this year's report which indicates that the government is barely able to keep abreast with the newly created demand for houses.
It is true that one of the bottlenecks that have created the housing shortage is the shortage of mortgage funds, and apparently the sole purpose of the changes introduced into the National Housing Act by this bill is to try to overcome that shortage with the distinct understanding, I presume, on the part of the government, that if only that difficulty can be met, if only money can be made available for mortgage funds, our housing problem will be solved. Many other factors enter into the solution of the housing problem than the amount of mortgage funds available.

I shall try to deal with some of the principles of the bill. I shall try to present my criticism of them and make what I hope the government will consider constructive suggestions for improvement, although on that latter point I must say that I have not very much hope. First let us look at the proposal to insure mortgages. The principle underlying mortgage insurance is that the lending institutions can receive an insurance payment, in reality a debenture guaranteed by the government, upon the transfer of the mortgaged property to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The corporation is to be empowered to buy insured mortgages from approved investment institutions, and when the Bank Act and the Bank of Canada Act come up for revision insurance mortgages will be made acceptable security for Bank of Canada advances to chartered banks in the same way as government bonds are today.
When lending agencies are insured by the government against investment risk, and incidentally they will be insured by the borrowers who will pay the additional insurance premium, investment companies will no longer have to worry about any loss likely to be sustained through the business of lending money on houses. They can then content themselves entirely with the business of making profits out of the housing problem. Should a loan fall into default the approved lender is then expected to secure title to the mortgaged property and to convey such title to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The approved lender will then be paid in cash 98 per cent of the sum of the principal outstanding at the date of conveyance plus interest up to six months at the mortgage interest rate, or in certain cases possibly up to twelve months, plus the borrower's charges, whatever they may amount to, plus a maximum of $125 for the transfer fee, plus whatever legal expenses may be incurred.
On the whole one of these insured mortgages presents fairly good security to the lending institution. What in effect happens is that the borrower is subsidizing the lending institution against almost the total risk despite the fact that the same institutions will be charging an interest rate which should in itself be a sufficient reward for the risk that these companies take. If the fundamental principle of the free enterprise system, which is so proudly acclaimed in this house by supporters of that system, lies in the expectation of profits as a reward for risk in investment, then this insurance feature which removes the risk seems to create somewhat of an ironical situation for the private enterprise system.
National Housing Act
Here we have a government which believes in the free enterprise system and believes that housing should be left as a preserve for free enterprise, which supports the theory that free enterprisers put their money into an enterprise and assume the risk on the basis of some profits, at the same time calling upon the borrower or home purchaser, through an added insurance premium, to secure such private enterprises against risk and loss. Mortgage insurance is unquestionably provided solely for the protection of the lending institutions against loss in the event that a purchaser should default in his payments or in the event of a recession taking place during which recession any considerable number of purchasers may be forced to default in their payments.
There is not the slightest indication in the bill that the government has given one moment's consideration to any protection for the original purchaser of a property. There is no protection whatever for the equity that a purchaser may have in a property when circumstances force him to default and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation obtains possession of the property. Moreover, I think that the protection provided under these insurance policies is entirely unnecessary. It is unnecessary protection for the lender and it creates an additional cost to the purchaser.
I notice that the government does not want to assume directly the unpopular responsibility of foreclosing mortgages in default. It leaves that unpopular responsibility to the original lenders. Nevertheless, the government becomes, indirectly, a party to these foreclosures. The only possible good that I can see resulting from the protection afforded by the mortgage insurance principle is, as I said before, the unnecessary protection for lending institutions.
Since I presume some such measure as this is necessary if the banks are to be induced to depart from their ordinary practice and put money into mortgages, possibly some new mortgage money will be made available. Whether or not the amount of money the banks can be induced, under this legislation, to put into the general mortgage pool will be more than the government withdraws from the pool by terminating its joint lending policy, or whether it will be enough to make any appreciable difference in the number of houses that will be built, remains to be seen. I notice that the bankers are a bit cagey about going into this business. In this morning's Globe and Mail, the president of the Bank of Toronto is reported to have said that it is only to a moderate extent

National Housing Act that it would be prudent tor a bank to tie up the funds of Canadian depositors in longterm fixed investments. The president of the Bank of Toronto has a good deal more along the same lines in that speech.
We may possibly get a little more mortgage money. Even if we do succeed in getting more mortgage money into the mortgage pool from the banks, that in itself is not going to solve the housing problem. I do not think it is necessary to introduce this insurance principle into our housing legislation in order to insure the liquidity of the small proportion that the banks are likely to put into the mortgage pool. It has been estimated by responsible authorities that the banks are not likely, in any case, to put more than 5 per cent of their available money into mortgages. I doubt if it is necessary to charge the purchaser of every home an additional insurance premium in order to safeguard that small proportion of mortgage money.
So far as the life insurance companies and trust companies are concerned, they have not been doing too badly in the past so far as mortgage loans are concerned. The fact that this legislation may induce banks to go into the mortgage pool, and even though we may get an abundance of mortgage money, that is not going to make it possible for those in the lower income groups to procure homes. We must take other measures. Even if we extend the amortization period to 40 or even 50 years, and thereby reduce the monthly payment on houses, there will still remain a large sector of the Canadian people who will not be able to secure homes. It is true that by some such measure as that we may be able to make it possible for those in the $3,000 bracket or those in the $2,500 bracket to purchase homes, whereas now they are excluded from that possibility. Even under those circumstances we shall still have well over 50 per cent of the wage earners of Canada unable to purchase homes.
I suggest that instead of terminating the joint lending principle under which the government has been operating in the past the government should, as we in this group have suggested many times, issue loans directly to borrowers through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and set up a special revolving fund for that purpose. I fail to see the need for this government adding to the cost of houses through this mortgage insurance principle, and depending for mortgage money on private institutions. So far as I am concerned, housing is just as great a social need in this country as schools and


many other public services. If the government is to meet this need to any extent that will be satisfactory to the people of this country, then I say that instead of getting out of the mortgage business the government should get back into it directly by means of a revolving fund.
In a recent editorial the Globe and Mail took members of this house to task for always talking about the housing situation but never really doing anything about it or suggesting anything constructive. According to the Globe and Mail one factor in housing that we seem to overlook is the high cost of houses. So far as that newspaper is concerned, the way to reduce the high cost of houses is to reduce wages. Apparently the Globe and Mail feels that members of parliament should advocate drastic reductions in wages in the building trades and in other trades in order to bring down the price of houses to within reach of people in the lower income brackets. We in the C.C.F. have suggested before one means of reducing the cost of houses to purchasers, and that is a reduction in the interest rate.
I have pointed out a number of times in this house that a reduction of 50 per cent in the interest rate will do more to reduce the carrying charges on a house than a 50 per cent reduction in the cost of labour and materials.
Again, we criticize this bill because no fixed interest rate is stated. The interest rate may vary, and apparently it may go as high as 5} per cent or even 6 per cent. Again I suggest that the government should make money available for housing at not more than 2 per cent. That, in itself, will do more to reduce carrying charges on houses, and to make houses available to those in the lower income groups, than any other measure we could take.
If the government wants to maintain the present interest rate, then I suggest that it should subsidize the interest rate on housing, as a social service to the country, or at least that it should subsidize the interest rate on housing below a certain cost, in order that, through that means, we may make houses available to more people in the lower income groups. If the government does not want to subsidize the interest rate on housing, then I suggest that it use the facilities of the Bank of Canada to provide money for housing at the rate of 2 per cent.
I see no reason why the limitation of $8,000 should be placed in the bill before 90 per cent of the lending value can be secured. I suggest that instead of limiting the 90 per cent lending value to $8,000, that figure should

be raised to $12,000. Today it is practically impossible to purchase a bungalow in the Toronto district for much less than $12,000. I suggest the act should permit a loan of 90 per cent on houses with a lending value up to $12,000. If the government would agree to a lower interest rate, then I would be all in favour of a longer amortization period than is provided in the bill.
There is no new change in the legislation, so far as low-rental housing is concerned. Low-rental housing presents one of the great needs of our time. There are and there will be a great many people who just cannot afford to buy or to build homes, even under the most favourable conditions. There are and will continue to be many people who will have recourse to renting homes, if they are to have homes at all. And for that lower income group who cannot afford to buy or to build homes, I suggest that the government should establish a rental subsidy fund.
The present legislation provides means whereby the government may enter into partnership with a provincial government or a municipality in sharing the cost of building and the cost of maintenance. However, I can find nothing in the legislation whereby the federal government undertakes to make any provision for a reduction in the rent below the economic level.
If those houses are to be available, then they must be available to the people on the basis of their income, and not on the basis of an economic rental. Somebody must then be able to make up the difference between the rent charged and what would constitute an economic rental. I suggest that if the government is to meet the low-rental housing problem, it should set up a low-rental subsidy fund for that purpose.
One of the drawbacks in connection with housing, as the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) pointed out, is the difficulty that municipalities have in providing serviced land and schools for new subdivisions. I suggest that any legislation which attempts to meet the present housing need should make some provision whereby the federal government could come to the assistance of the municipalities, through the provincial governments, for the building of schools and the provision of serviced land.
So long as we fail to face up to this problem, the municipalities will remain very reluctant to participate in the provisions of the act which are made available for that purpose. I have no particular objection to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation undertaking to fix the appraisal value of the loan. As a matter of fact I think it is likely 83276-85
National Housing Act
to work out much fairer than the present arrangement. I have heard builders say that they find, by experience, it is much more satisfactory to deal with Central Mortgage than to deal with the private lending institutions. In spite of all that has been said about government red tape, as applied to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, experienced builders have told me that there is far more red tape in getting a loan through private lending institutions than when dealing with Central Mortgage.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the house rose at six o'clock I had attempted to show features of Bill No. 102 to which I objected, to give reasons for my objection, and to put forward certain constructive suggestions which in my opinion would serve to meet the needs of Canadian people with regard to housing.
I shall now take the few minutes remaining to give a summary of these suggestions. My first suggestion was that the principle of mortgage insurance be rejected on the ground that it imposes an unnecessary burden on prospective Canadian home owners and unnecessary protection to finance institutions. I have no particular objection to the banks going into the mortgage business if they find it profitable to do so.
My second suggestion is that instead of withdrawing completely from the lending field in favour of private enterprise the government, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, should issue loans directly to the borrower and should set up a special revolving fund for that purpose.
My third suggestion was that such loans should bear a fixed interest rate, and not be tied to a varying factor as is the case in the bill.
My fourth suggestion was that that fixed interest rate should be 2 per cent, a rate which we in the C.C.F. have advocated in this house and which we advocated on the hustings during the election campaign. I suggested that in order to achieve that 2 per cent interest rate the government might either use the facilities of the Bank of Canada or subsidize interest rates for houses, particularly for the lower priced houses.

National Housing Act
My fifth suggestion was that the amount of the loan should be 90 per cent of the lending value up to $12,000, instead of the $8,000 imposed by the present bill.
My sixth suggestion was that, provided that the interest rate is lowered, the amortization period be increased to 30 years instead of 25 as is proposed in the new legislation.
My seventh suggestion was that in order to provide for those Canadians in the lower income brackets who cannot afford to buy or build houses, even under the most favourable conditions, the government should set up a rental subsidy fund which would assist in establishing a sharp reduction in the present rate of rent for those particular Canadians.
My last suggestion was that the federal government, in order to assist municipalities to take advantage of the provisions of this bill, should make grants to the provinces to be turned over to the municipalities for the purpose of constructing schools and other public facilities which are a heavy expense at the present time on the municipality wherever a new housing project is undertaken.
I might add that I have no particular objection-as a matter of fact I welcome it -to the change by reason of which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation undertakes to carry out inspection of houses built with the aid of loans under the National Housing Act. Much of the criticism which I have heard about the houses built under the National Housing Act originated from the improper or inadequate system of inspection which is carried on at the present time. I have met numerous purchasers of houses who have complained of the fact that the houses which they bought were not built up to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation standards. I have raised that question with Central Mortgage and Housing only to be assured that this inspection is left to the lending institution. I am quite confident that under Central Mortgage and Housing inspection we shall have a more satisfactory and a better system of inspection that will be in the interest of the buyers.
These are the constructive suggestions, Mr. Speaker, which I submit as alternatives to the measures contained in the present housing bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, frequently of recent date we have been accused by government members of not congratulating them on things that they have done. It was possibly an oversight on our part. We were so used to hearing them


congratulating themselves that we did not think it was completely necessary. However, at this time, I do congratulate the minister on bringing in such a fine piece of legislation; that is, in recognizing the need of reform in this particular legislation, and on dealing with it so well and so completely, and, if I may say so, so briefly.
I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) on doing such an excellent job of providing a summary of what the minister gave us, but at some great length, and in such a way as to show the pitfalls into which we may find ourselves were we to adopt this particular scheme.
I would also congratulate the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), who, in his particular case, recognizing the fallacy of the socialistic way of doing things, apparently is even willing to allow our borrowing money from banks at 2 per cent interest.
On three vital points that interest me I think the minister is to be commended. First, the government recognizes the vital need for housing. Second, the government recognizes the need of improving older homes. Third, the government is trying to provide means of financing those homes. I think those are three most important essentials.
However, the object of an opposition is, first, to be critical because we have to protect the taxpayer; and, second, to suggest alternatives to what is proposed.
I am led to believe from the bill that the government probably has read certain press clippings in which frequent mention was made that incomes and savings are up. We know that incomes are up. There is no doubt that the wage earner in Canada earns more money today than ever before. But we are told also that 83-4 per cent of the population of Canada earns less than $3,000 a year.
However, the purchasing power of the dollar is down to less than 50 per cent. Savings may be up, but it is not the little man, it is not the millworker, it is not the clerk, it is not the dock worker who has the money; it is the fellow who had a little extra money beforehand that has some today. But he has not enough to invest in a home and the minister recognizes that fact by lowering the down payment.
I submit that the down payment proposed in the bill is still too high. The down payment of 10 per cent on the first $8,000 is quite equitable, but when you start adding 30 per cent above that it results in just too much money for the ordinary individual. The need for housing is quite apparent. For instance, I have a clipping from the Ottawa Journal of January 14 which tells of a family of four

in Brockville who were nearly frozen because they had to live in a tent. Hon. members probably saw that article. Then to go to the Pacific coast, I find the following in the British Columbian of Tuesday, January 12, 1954:
Family offered basement
The plight of a Dutch immigrant family of eight threatened with eviction from their small Surrey home has been answered by a Burnaby resident.
I am happy that the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) are both here to help in providing a residence for this family.

I received, as I think most British Columbia members did, a letter from the acting mayor of the city of Vancouver enclosing a brief which had been sent to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), and which I think was formally sent on to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). I contend that housing conditions such as these should not prevail in a country like ours.
If I may digress for a moment I should like to indicate the growth of housing in the area which I represent, and when I refer to housing I do not mean under the National Housing Act. I want to tell of what has been done by the little fellow, the man with whom 8327&-85J	[DOT]' v:-JL-aia*

I am so familiar. Following the war many of these men wanted a home; they needed accommodation but they could not afford to buy a home under the National Housing Act. Many times the man in this category found that his wages were too low. He did not have job security. He did not have enough money to make a down payment. As the result of those factors he built a cheap domicile of some kind. But by so doing he depreciated the value of the surrounding; properties, and that is an important factor-The values of those homes are still being, depreciated on the resale market. If this; man had built in a shack region he would simply be helping to build up a slum area.
That man's present needs are enhanced because his house has deteriorated. Most likely he was a married man, and in all probability his family has increased and he requires more space. At this point I should like to give credit to the builders of British Columbia, particularly the supply houses, who foresaw this difficulty and took it upon themselves to try to help those people by offering service loans up to $2,000.
However, the rates of interest were exorbitant, and the time of repayment being a matter of two years, it was impractical and it is impractical today so far as these people are concerned. They are not wealthy and what they receive from their work is not sufficient to permit them to repay such a loan, as well as taxes and other expenses they may have.
As I read the bill, it contains an arrangement whereby a man building a home may do some work on it and can apply that to the loan. The bill is not too clear, but I wonder whether or not the man who was constructing a home could work on that home himself and have. that apply on the down payment, or at least a certain portion of it. I think that might be worthy of consideration.
As I said earlier, the down payment is still too high. The Vancouver Province of January 5, 1954, carried the results of a questionnaire which had been sent out by a fact-finding committee. The purpose was to find out what the people on the Pacific coast were willing to pay for homes. Here are some pertinent facts with regard to the rate of interest. An article in the Vancouver Province, dated January 5, 1954, states:
It is quite evident that one cannot get much of a house for even $10,000 plus the lot at today's building costs, which, again, is inflated owing to lack of serviced land.
Earlier the article states:
The present proposal "is not the answer for those in the lower income brackets because our building by-laws do not permit semi-detached or row housing here."

National Housing Act
It goes on:
. . . the act should be based on a straight 10 per cent down on $12,000 to be of use to the average citizen.
In a questionnaire published the same day in the same newspaper certain suggestions were made and members of the public were invited to answer this questionnaire. For example, the first question is:
In your opinion should the municipalities and the federal government jointly finance clearing and servicing of land making reasonably priced building lots available under the terms already provided for in the National Housing Act?
The answer given on an average was: Yes.
The final tabulation of these facts and figures on this question has not yet been completed but the trend is shown and that trend is "yes". There is one feature we must definitely consider and that is the matter of exploitation. Exploitation must be stopped. The workingman, or any man for that matter, intent on building a home should not have to pay an exorbitant price for a piece of property, nor should he have to pay more than the lumber and building materials were worth to start with. That does not mean that a businessman should not get his proper rate of profit. No man can live without profit. The workingman would not have a job unless the businessman had his profit. But we must see to it that the buyer is not exploited.
The second question was:
Has the high down payment barred you from home ownership?
The answer is "Yes".
As I said earlier, the minister is to be congratulated on reducing the down payment, although I do not believe he has reduced it far enough. The third question is:
If a lower down payment results from the changes in the National Housing Act do you intend to build?
The answer again was "Yes". I would therefore expect, Mr. Speaker, that the act will be used to full advantage in the city of Vancouver. The fourth question was:
What is the largest amount you can afford for a down payment?
The figure arrived at was $1,200. I do not know how many hon. members are in business but I left my business to come to Ottawa to help look after the nation's business. I was in the credit business and I always found that if a man asked for a loan of $50 he could only afford to repay $40. Most people overstep the mark and if they say they can afford a $1,200 down payment, then it is almost certain they can afford only $1,000. Their imagination runs away with them and they overlook the fact they have other things to consider besides the down payment.
