The next question was:
What monthly repayment could you afford?
The answer in this case was $55 to $60.
In this instance the same comparison applies. If they cannot afford $1,200 as a down payment, they cannot afford $55 or $60 a month either. It is true many people are paying that amount but they cannot afford it. Their homes are suffering. The average wage earner does not get enough per month to be able to afford a repayment of from $55 to $60 per month, and it is quite certain that most of these people have not allowed for such incidentals as roofing repairs, painting that may have to be done, or even income tax and medical expenses.
As regards a question of inflation, there is one factor here we should note, particularly in regard to the down payment mentioned earlier, and that is that the Americans provide homes for a down payment as low as $500. I do not know whether the minister and his colleagues have studied the United States housing plan, but I imagine they will have done so and I hope that as a result of their investigations we can expect lower down payments than are proposed under this act.
One of the most important things in life so far as owning a home is concerned is the fact that we must have security in tenancy. By that I mean that an owner must feel assured when he buys that he is going to be able to hold on to his home. He does not want to be constantly haunted by the fear that he is going to lose it at any time. I am very pleased to see that the amortization period may be extended from 25 to 30 years because that is one of the factors that will decrease monthly payments.
One other factor to consider is the rate of interest. It was dealt with in some degree by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy). The rate he suggests is 2 per cent. I imagine in this particular instance he was referring to something that is true only of the Social Credit province of Alberta where they have a 2 per cent revolving fund which is used to make community projects self-liquidating. I do not believe that is necessarily true in this instance for the simple reason that under the housing scheme now proposed the banks, which are privately owned institutions, must have some degree of profit. They exist on profit.
Under the proposal as it now stands we have an insurance scheme which will guard them against any loss; but if we are going to allow them something I think it will have

to be a little more than 2 per cent, because 2 per cent will probably not pay for the cost of handling the funds.
I do not know where the hon. member got the 2 per cent figure from, but I do know that in all likelihood the facts will prove that the 2 per cent charge is not sufficient to cover the cost of handling the large sums of money to be used.
However, let us suppose we give the banks a profit of 1J per cent plus the other 2 per cent which would give them 3J per cent. One hundred thousand units built, not at an average cost of $10,700, but at $10,000, would give the banks a net profit of $15 million. I know $15 million is not a good return on an investment of $1 billion as far as the businessman is concerned, but the banks owe something to the Canadian people. They must recognize that fact. As a grocer I would be expected to have a certain range of loss leader goods and if I did not have them people would walk down to the nearest chain store to get them. As a garage man I am expected to give free air. In the same way the banker is expected to do something more for the people than just to take a profit. Opposed to this 3J, per cent we have the suggestion that the interest may be as high as 6 per cent. That would mean something like $60 million profit for the banks on an average $10,000 home, 100,000-unit project. That would be the regular rate of interest. Mind you, I do not think the rate will be that high. I think it was mentioned that was considered too high a figure and therefore should not be the one to be used.
I think all hon. members are conversant with the saying of that famous statesman who said, some years ago, "Give us the tools and we will finish the job." We have the tools and we have the job. Apparently all we lack at the present moment is the initiative to put the two together with a few millions or billions of dollars to complete the job. There are statements by certain individuals of national stature which we must refute. I would refer to one, R. E. G. Davis, director of the Canadian Welfare Council, who said, as reported in the Financial Times of November 26, 1953:
The shape and composition of our towns and cities at present, and of our new neighbourhoods springing up overnight in the suburbs are being determined not by any rational consideration of how to provide the best living conditions for people, but almost solely by what will bring the largest profit to the building and shopping interests that have the development in hand. We shall never make progress so long as this situation continues and one of our first objectives must be to see it is quickly brought to an end.
National Housing Act
Hon. members will notice these words- "almost solely by what will bring the largest profits to the building and shopping interests that have the development in hand." It is very important that we should protect ourselves against anything like that, and statements of this type must be challenged. It is a simple matter to tear things to pieces but it is quite a different thing to try to improve them. Therefore in this particular case I have a suggestion that I should like to pass on to our good friend, the minister. It is one that was adopted by another country, and undoubtedly the minister has studied it. He may even have a complete answer to the reason it has not been considered at greater length.
I speak of the experience of Brazil. Between 1933 and 1940 Brazil had a nation-wide depression similar to ours, and private enterprise Brazilian builders carried out this plan. They formulated a housing project that has resulted in between 70 and 75 per cent of the people of Brazil owning their own homes today compared with the figure of 65 per cent quoted for Canada. This result was achieved during the time when Brazilian banks were paying 7 per cent on demand savings. At that time I believe our Canadian banks were paying 3 per cent. I am not sure, but I believe that is the figure. All the bankers, builders and everyone else concerned in the project in Brazil made money. That is a very important feature; everyone concerned made money. There is a distinction to be made between the lending of money already in existence and the creation of new money. The minister knows that in Canada new money is created practically at will. Every time we have a large wheat crop we get an additional crop of new money with which to purchase the surplus immediately. Mind you, that is not true today because we cannot sell all of the surplus to ourselves. But during the years when we had elevator space available new money was created to help business along and look after it properly.
The secret of the success of the Brazilian scheme lies with the Brazilian government itself. Instead of waiting for the people of Brazil to borrow money from private interests, the Brazilian treasury issued certificates which we might compare to deposit certificates. These certificates were equal to the value of the materials and labour involved in the particular housing project. We must first remember that the purpose of the whole scheme was to take care of the unemployment then prevalent in Brazil, and there was

National Housing Act
also the factor that they had such a large surplus of goods on hand which they wanted to get rid of.
These deposit certificates were handed to the chartered banks and the chartered banks loaned them to accredited contractors at a rate of 2 per cent. At the same time the savings banks were paying 7 per cent the chartered banks were lending this money to builders at the rate of 2 per cent. The builders constructed the buildings and in turn sold them to the prospective buyers who repaid the chartered banks the actual cost of the homes on a monthly basis plus a 2 per cent carrying charge. This plan put people in Brazil back to work, as it was supposed to do. It also solved the housing problem. Houses are the means whereby we stabilize the economy of the country, and if the depression that some people seem to expect should become a reality we might well consider having such a project.
In a matter of ten to fifteen years prospective Brazilian home owners had become home owners. There was no down payment involved in the scheme. It might be asked what the banks did when the loans were repaid. They sent the certificates back to the treasury which destroyed them. We find that in that instance the people of Brazil used their labour and surplus materials to excellent advantage without its costing them an exorbitant rate of interest such as the 5i per cent rate we have today, or 6 per cent, as the case may be. I am reminded of a statement made earlier that the interest rate is not a fixed rate. I believe it should be fixed because the prospective home owner entering into negotiations should know what he is going to have to pay.
Under the Brazilian scheme 2 per cent was the cost of handling the certificates, and perhaps our banks should do the same thing in an identical fashion. We have the institutions already in existence. We need homes, and we have the materials. H. R. MacMillan, the lumber magnate of the Pacific coast, said the other day that we have no market for our lumber. I do not know whether or not everyone realizes it, but the British Columbia export business is built on a basis whereby no country takes more than 10 per cent of our export surplus for its home market. Such an amount would mean nothing as far as the market requirements of any foreign nation are concerned, and we could very easily lose such markets completely if these countries chose to reduce their imports from Canada by 10 per cent.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I believe I have put the case very clearly in so far as the proposal I have in mind is concerned. I would go on

to summarize my ideas in this way. First and foremost, we must curb inflation in building costs. It is necessary that the price of homes stops rising, and that we keep that price at a level which everyone can afford. I should like to impress upon the minister also the need for allowing the value of the labour used in the construction of these homes to be construed as a down payment. It is necessary, too, to ascertain whether or not it is possible to reduce the interest rate from the 5 per cent or 6 per cent that is suggested to a nominal figure such as 3-5 per cent.
I know that under the insurance scheme, which I have not discussed, it is going to require 2 per cent to carry the insurance premiums, and there would be an additional 2 per cent to cover the cost of operation of the banks, so that might mean a total of 4 per cent. I believe, however, it is the purpose of the banks to look after the community and to help in the building of Canada which is so essential at this time. I would ask in all seriousness that not only the minister but everyone in this house study very closely the Brazilian method of building homes from 1933 to 1940, when they actually kept their unemployed busy and got rid of their surplus goods by monetizing the wealth of the nation.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of this bill, the purpose of which is to promote the construction of new homes and improve the living conditions in this country. During the last election campaign I promised my own constituents of Brantford that I would press for new legislation of the kind that is now before us. I note that the government, in its appeal to the people for support, did not make any promises whatever along those lines but I felt a keen personal interest in the whole matter and allowed myself to go on record in favour of a new housing act.
I believe that the government is to be congratulated on bringing forward this bill so early in the session after the last election. The legislation which is before us, and which will replace the National Housing Act now in force, is breaking new ground in Canada so far as progressive legislation is concerned. In my view what we are embarking upon is a forward step, and it ought to have far-reaching and beneficial consequences. We are all agreed on one thing-at least I do not believe any member in this house doubts it- that there is still a need for more and better housing in this great country of ours. The question is, does this legislation meet our needs; and, more important still, is it sound?
Some hon. members might feel quite sincerely that the bill does not go far enough,

and in particular that a flat 10 per cent down payment should have been provided on every house constructed under the act costing up to $12,000 to $15,000. Upon first consideration, I might have been of this view, but on sober second thought, Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe that the provisions contained in the bill are sound; that the legislation is wise and ought to be supported. We are engaged in a new venture. The government is striving to place some of the available credit of the country behind the man who is embarking on that greatest endeavour of all, the founding of a home of his own. Most of us in the house, I am sure, believe that the great majority of Canadians ought to own their own homes. In my view this is of necessity a basic feature of our society.
If Canada is going to be great and strong, strong at home and abroad; if we are going to make a contribution to the world of today; then this nation of ours must be a nation of home owners. If a man can own real estate, part of the soil of Canada, and construct a house thereon under the provisions of this act, he thereupon has a genuine stake in the welfare and future of our country. This is one of the reasons this bill is so important, and why its effects may be far-reaching.
Most of the young men and women of our land need the assistance of some form of credit in order to establish themselves in life. That is what this bill provides. I do not think the majority of young men and women in Canada want handouts from the government. They need assistance in the form of loans which they can pay off. They want to own a home of their own, and to pay for that home. In this way they hope to acquire a little independence of that type which has been enjoyed by our fathers and forefathers in this country since the beginning. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I am going to support this bill. I believe it to be a move genuinely designed to promote home ownership from one end of the country to the other.
Does this legislation go far enough? In the election campaign I suggested a 10 per cent down payment be made available. Now, that has been done in this act. If a man desires to construct a $12,000 home or a $16,000 home, would it be wise for him to borrow up to 90 per cent of that large sum? Could he afford to keep up the resultant heavy monthly payments under such a scheme? Should this government give him encouragement by providing in this bill for his doing so? I do not think so. Would it be wise for any man to assume an obligation that would take a period of more than 25 years to amortize under normal repayment
National Housing Act
terms? Should the government have encouraged him to do that? Again, I say I do not think so.
What concerns me in connection with this bill is not reducing the amount of the down payment below what is provided or extending the term of tenure of the mortgage. What is concerning me is this: will the bill result in loans becoming more available to the average citizen? That is the question which is paramount; that is the question on which this bill should stand or fall.
The trouble in the past has been, at least in my view and in my experiences from day to day in a law practice, that satisfactory loans have been too difficult to attain. The provision in this legislation to make available insured loans, through the banks, in my opinion should open the door to much greater credit facilities for the average man and woman in Canada.
I do not think the bill should be opposed simply because some of its terms do not satisfy some hon. members. Let us give the legislation before us a fair trial for, say, two years, thus giving at least an opportunity to ascertain if in practice it will have the effect we want it to have, and that we hope it will have.
If housing loans become more available to the general public than they have been in the past, then this bill will have amply fulfilled its purpose and will have justified the basic idea which prompted the government to bring in the legislation at the present time.
Like many other hon. members on this side of the house I was very much puzzled and, indeed, shocked by the speech of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), who spoke on behalf of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. I am sorry he is not in the house tonight. It is not for me to comment upon the speech of one who holds the esteem of all parties in the house, and who is a very powerful figure in the Conservative opposition. But it was impossible for me to ascertain whether he and his party were for the bill or were against it.
At any rate, it may be that he and his party have not quite made up their minds. He did utter some valuable warnings as to the possible results which might ensue from the passage of the bill, but he offered no substitute and brought forward no other proposal on behalf of his party to take the place of this legislation.
Returning to the bill, I am glad that it will make possible a better service than has ever been available before to the residents of small centres and remote communities across Canada. It is a great forward step.

National Housing Act
Instead of having to deal by correspondence with lending companies, the people will be in a position to consult the nearest branch bank manager, and to talk over their problems with him. This will be a great convenience.
The hon. member for Eglinton thought that the banks would not co-operate; I think they will. I believe that it will be of the greatest convenience to the people who live in the remote communities and smaller centres in our country. I have in mind, in particular, my own good city of Brantford, which I am proud to represent in the House of Commons. Then, we also have people in the township of Burford, a truly splendid community in my constituency, who, I believe, will be vitally affected by the passage of this legislation. In spite of what the hon. member for Eglinton has said, it could be that they will be able to go to those two historic little villages of Burford and Scotland, and there discuss with their bank managers the vital problem of housing, which concerns all those people.
The people in these communities are in my view the very backbone of Canada. They are sure to derive lasting benefits from this legislation. I hope that when the measure reaches the committee stage the individual sections will receive careful and thorough study, particularly with respect to the provisions relating to interest rates.
I repeat that the government ought to be congratulated upon bringing forward legislation of the kind proposed in this bill. In my view it deserves and eventually will have the support of a large majority of members in the house, of whatever party, who are sincerely desirous of promoting the well-being of our country in a substantial and material way.

I want to conclude my remarks in the beautiful tongue of my French-Canadian colleagues, whom I have been so happy to know since my arrival in Ottawa.
In my opinion the bill now before the house should obtain the support of the majority of hon. members. I see in it a sincere effort on the part of the government to help the man who would like to start on the most important undertaking of his life, that of acquiring his own house and establishing a family.
I am confident that this measure will contribute toward increasing the possibilities open to Canadian citizens and widening their horizons.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I first read the outline of the bill I was


under the impression that its purpose was to promote the construction of homes as well as to improve housing and living conditions. I had been led to believe that within its framework we would find the means whereby the government would place the purchase of homes within the reach of low income families, and make it possible for them to grasp this offer of help.
This bill, heralded as a boon to ameliorate the plight of the family in the low income group, that vast host of our population in which the heads of families are receiving incomes less than $3,500 per year, does not measure up to what we had expected. Because of its many financial gyrations, the results of the bill must remain elusive.
After listening to the minister's comprehensive explanation of the proposals contained in the bill, it now becomes obvious that its paramount object and intent is to procure a greater reservoir of money to be made available for loans. It would seem that the chief concern in framing the bill has been to persuade those with funds-in this instance the banks-to enter an arena of financing from which heretofore they had been barred.
It now becomes evident that the banks were reluctant to take this step, and we now see that they are being catapulted into this service. They have been lured into an acceptance cf the situation through a process of making the major proposal attractive to them through the introduction of the new feature of insuring loans on terms of a 2 per cent payment, single premium. This is payable by the purchaser and is to be included in the monthly payments, thus making the attraction more effective.
Let us now pay some attention to the individual for whom the bill was devised. I refer to the purchaser in the low income group. We see at once how he has been manoeuvred into the position where, unless the government can be induced to re-admit him to the benefits involved, he cannot enjoy the provisions planned for him.
Under the present act-and I have been unable to find anything in the new proposals that removes the frustrations that the purchaser, who is in the income group earning below $3,500 a year, has encountered-the situation is this. Take the figure the minister has given, $10,000, as the price of a house, with the down payment of 14 per cent or $1,420, with the balance of $8,580 to be borrowed and the loan processed at 51 per cent, amortized in 25 years. The amortization schedule for this loan is $5.96 a month per thousand, amounting to a monthy payment of

$51. The rate on the same loan amortized at 30 years is $5.49 a month per thousand, or $46.70 a month.
The same figures for a $12,000 loan, which is the lowest price of a home today, works out, with the down payment of 14 per cent, at $1,680, with a balance of $10,320 at 5J per cent to be amortized in 25 years at $5.96 a month per thousand, or a monthly payment of $60.38. When amortized in 30 years at $5.49 a month per thousand, there is a payment of $56.50 a month. To these payments of $51 and $46.70 a month, amortized at 25 and 30 years respectively on a $10,000 home and payments of $60.38 and $56.50 a month amortized at 25 and 30 years respectively on a $12,000 home must be added the insurance charge to secure the lender's loan. There must also be added the taxes, say $180 a year, or $15 a month extra.
The house will note that these payments range from $46.70, $51, $56.50 to $60.38 per month, with $15 for taxes and 60 cents for loan insurance to be added, and are to be paid from an income below $3,500 a year or a maximum of $70 a week. This is where the frustration is brought about.
The lenders will not lend unless the purchaser has an assured income of over $4,200 a year, or $80 a week. Therefore, unless the present impediment is removed and the salary requirements are made favourable to the low income purchaser, this much-heralded bill becomes futile so far as it affects those for whom it was supposed to be designed. I will go one step further and predict that if you put a favourable salary requirement into effect for the low income group the price of the resale house will automatically come down.
Now, while I am on this phase of it I may say that I cannot see why the purchaser should be called upon to pay the single premium to insure and secure the loan advanced by the lender. I think the lending organizations would be willing to pay for the added protection. However, the amount is insignificant when spread over 25 or 30 years. Nevertheless, if you can set up a provision such as this for the lender, then the mechanics of the operation can be set up in favour of the purchaser for the same 2 per cent payment of a single premium, to be paid in the same way by the purchaser as he does for the insurance on the lender's loan. It will give a break to the one who has to carry the burden of the quarter of a century ahead in establishing a home, and it will give peace of mind to his family, keep a roof over their heads, and give added security should misfortune overtake the breadwinner.
National Housing Act
I say this because the burden on the purchaser seems to be given the least consideration in this bill. All the other considerations are given to those who are going to benefit the most from the profit that is to be obtained from it. The man who seems to be forgotten in this bill is the one that I should like to draw to the attention of the minister, to see if something can be done to permit him to purchase a home.
As I say, the bill was originally designed to help the purchaser; but when these restrictions are placed upon him, it means that when a man goes to purchase a home he is confronted with a situation of such magnitude that he cannot possibly get loans from the lending companies. When I asked the minister questions when he first introduced this bill that was the thought that I had in mind. I was thinking of the individual who is in the low income bracket and who I hoped would secure the benefits of this bill, which have been denied to him. I should like the minister to study this matter further to see if he cannot find some way of reducing the salary requirements insisted upon by the lenders and give a prospective purchaser the advantages intended.

speechtext:
regret that when I spoke in the house last fall I was unable to do as many other hon. members did, namely, to spend a few minutes speaking of the beauties of the area that I represent. One of the reasons why I was unable to speak in that vein was the policies of the government in regard to housing. My riding consists partly of hundreds and hundreds of tar paper shacks, and I lay the blame -I think fairly-on the shoulders of this government. The suburban ridings have been most harshly discriminated against in the matter of housing legislation. The housing legislation where it has helped has helped the larger centres of population.
I feel that the old policies of the government were not sufficiently aggressive, and I notice that not only do we in British Columbia feel this way but so does Quebec. I noticed in the report of the Quebec board of trade to the royal commission of inquiry into constitutional problems the following on housing:
The home building policy of the federal government is not sufficiently aggressive and the shortage of housing units is still being felt.
We had another admission this afternoon from the minister that out of 105,000 houses that he thinks were built last year, only 40,000 used the facilities of the National Housing Act. In other words, more than one-half of the new housing units that were built in Canada were built without using the facilities of the National Housing Act.

National Housing Act
The National Housing Act was designed to make it easier for people to build houses. If it really were fulfilling this function I maintain that the percentage of houses and of housebuilders using these facilities should have been much larger.
The statement was made that for the first time we have been able to build as many new houses as new family units have been formed. That statement ignores the fact that in large areas of Canada we have now reached the stage where thousands of old houses are no longer fit for human use. That statement is subject to many qualifications. I hold in my hand an article which appeared in the January 16 issue of the British Columbian, a daily newspaper. The article says:
While there is slightly less substandard housing in the greater Vancouver area than there was at the end of the war, the total building program has not kept pace with new family formation and the influx of new families to the area: twenty thousand units short in 1945, housing accommodation falls even farther behind local needs today, particularly for low income families.
That is the consensus of opinion of the Vancouver Housing Association, which is a Red Feather agency. There is an admission in the Vancouver Sun of January 9 that in the Vancouver area housing has reached its second lowest point since 1947. It was stated that, in the Vancouver area, of the $50 million odd that went into new construction last year only $11 million or some 23 per cent went into housing. That percentage is far too low at a time when housing is of such paramount importance. To think that upwards of $39 million should go into other building while only $11 million went into housing!
I notice that the pinch is being felt not just in the larger urban centres. Right after the war every urban centre was faced with a serious housing shortage, but now from one end of Canada to the other every little hamlet, community and village has a housing shortage. The situation has not improved, it is getting worse. This is what has happened at a time when there is such a growing social need, at a time when we need to consume more in our dominion, at a time when we have surpluses of all primary materials, of inventories; at a time when there has been a slow-down in exports and when our national production is up. We are faced with a situation where housing difficulties are becoming worse. Every policy of this government should be aimed at using up more consumer goods by filling the need for homes.
I note the statement that the old National Housing Act was successful, but I cannot agree with that. It was not successful either in the joint lending set-up or in the other

sections. There was an arrangement for direct loans by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which has been referred to in glowing terms. However, I found throughout rural British Columbia that the common complaint about these direct loans was the long delay in servicing the loans. People had to wait half a year or more before a man even came out to look at their lots. That is hardly good enough.
If the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) thinks that by using the banks the people in the smaller communities will be helped he had better have another look at the bill. This bill will make loans even more subject to the approval of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The old act contained several provisions with regard to low rental housing and there was a section devoted to research. I maintain that on the whole those sections have been miserable failures. They have not been utilized to anywhere near the extent envisaged at the time the act was introduced.
A plea has been made that there should be a two-year trial of the new legislation. I submit that if we are going to have a breakdown in housing for two years, that is two years more than the Canadian people would like to see.
Reference has been made to the effective demand for housing and considerable weight seemed to be attached to that. I hope that before this bill passes there will be a clearer definition of what is meant by effective demand. Does effective demand refer only to those people who do not need the help of the government in connection with building homes or does it refer to those who really need homes?
The contention has been made that the housing scheme worked shortly after the end of world war II and then the Korean war came along and the rate of new house construction declined. It is admitted by those who are in the housing field that there has not been the upsurge since that there should be in this industry.
I am not one of those who like to be branded as irresponsible, who are ready to advocate anything. I realize that if we are going to build the 200,000 homes per year, which we must have as a minimum, the money must be found. I maintain that the only source of money is the increased purchasing power of the Canadian people. You can talk all you like 'of monetizing the nation's wealth, but the only thing you can monetize is that which has been obtained after labour has been applied to raw materials and the resulting product has not been

consumed. That is delayed purchasing power and it is the only money that I have any faith in.
Irrespective of the conditions that have been laid down, I feel that the government is attempting to pull out of this housing dilemma in a very odd way. They are hoping that Canadians do not know enough of this business of money to be able to lay the blame where it rightly belongs. I think they are hoping to use the chartered banks of Canada several years hence as a scapegoat and lay the blame on them for their unwillingness to do their share.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) outlined the plan for finding money that was exercised in Brazil. I was glad to note that he did not use Venezuela as an example, which at one time was held up as a model of Socred monetary theories. We now find that that is one of the worst authoritarian regimes in existence and they have now turned to one of the neighbouring nations and are using Brazil as an example. I noted the statement that if we have a depression this government might well consider a similar method of financing housebuilding in Canada.
The C.C.F. has always maintained that, in times of depression when those who have money are refusing to invest it, it is necessary for the government to take remedial action, and we would go along with the hon. member for New Westminster in saying "if we have a depression". But I think we must admit that that time has not arrived as yet. I note that he says also that first and foremost we must curb inflation. I am very pleased to hear that said by one of the members in their ranks. I am looking forward to the time when he will be moved up to one of the front seats in that organization, nearer the centre of the house. The people in my native province are looking forward to the day when those who say that they are first and foremost in favour of curbing inflation will be recognized.
The money must be found, and that is where the responsibility of the government enters in. I maintain that our insurance, mortgage and trust companies went on a strike against meeting our housing needs some seven months ago. They have been holding a gun to the head of the government year after year; they have persuaded or influenced the government to raise the interest rates. Last year they found that they could invest their money more safely elsewhere and receive a much higher rate of return. After all, the safety of money invested in a house is contingent upon the 83276-86i
National Housing Act
owner of the house being steadily employed at a favourable wage rate, and so forth. Money invested in oil lines is much more secure and the rate of return, sometimes guaranteed, is very much higher, so I cannot really blame those who are administering the insurance funds for seeking other and far more profitable lines of investment.
Ever since 1935, when they did it to win an election, the government has exercised a very strict control in Canada over the issuance of currency and credit throughout the nation. The time has now arrived when this government must assume its responsibilities in directing the investment funds of the nation. They are failing to assume that responsibility and are hoping the banks will help them out. We have had the most amazing admission that the available supply of money is tending to fall short, but the truth is that it is tending to fall short only in so far as the government is unwilling to direct the flow of investment money in the nation. The supply of money is more adequate than it ever was in Canadian history. One has only to look at the figures to substantiate that. Now we have the shift of responsibility to the banks. The insurance companies are going out of the business and so other fields are being looked for.
The banks, Mr. Speaker, if they are going to be of any real help to the nation in meeting the nation's housing needs, will have to curtail credit for the ordinary commercial needs of the nation. The only alternative is the liquidation by the banks of their government securities.
That in turn will have the effect of raising still higher the rate of interest the government will have to pay on future bond issues. I repeat, the only way in which the banks can adequately help is by curtailing the ordinary commercial needs of the nation.
There has been a lot said about the ability of the banks to help out. This statement has been made not in the house but in newspapers, and it is worth having a look at. The assets of the chartered banks of Canada as given on September 30 last were $10,398 million. Two hundred thousand homes would take $2 billion worth of mortgage money. Even if the banks were able to supply this money this year, next year they would receive a refund by way of repayment of only 3 or 4 per cent. If they harmed the commercial needs of the nation to the extent of $2 billion this year where would next year's $2 billion come from? There is only one logical source of housing money and that is the investment savings of the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate, I am not going to dwell on a lot of political theories nor take up the time of the house in that way. It seems we sometimes find that people think that the press gallery is fertile ground for the dissemination of political speeches. I believe the place for that is out on the hustings.
I am going to speak to you tonight for only a few minutes. I am not going to bring in a lot of figures which go in one ear and out the other and that do not mean too much. I know that the minister has access to far more statistics than most of us. It just depends upon the willingness of the government to use these statistics, so I feel there is no point in putting forth a lot of figures at this time.

National Housing Act
There is one point I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members, and I imagine there are quite a few who will agree with me. I believe that in considering this housing bill we should pay more attention to the man with a large family. It is a well recognized fact that the larger the family the larger the house, and the larger the house the more expensive it is to build. The man who has a large family naturally has greater responsibilities in rearing those children, and I believe therefore some consideration should be given to providing these large families with an opportunity to obtain a house equal to that given to the smaller family.
The thought I have in mind is that the down payment should never exceed 10 per cent because it is going to work a hardship on the individual who has a large family. Naturally, the individual with a larger family has something else to contend with that is greater than a person with a small family. I mean that the dining room table needs more plates around it; there need to be more beds in the house and there need to be more facilities all the way through. Speaking seriously, it is easily seen that a hardship is being worked on the individual who has the greatest responsibilities. I do not think the principle is right. Before I am through someone is going to realize that I have a large family.
I was a little bit concerned, Mr. Speaker, [DOT]over a press report appearing in the Montreal Gazette. I have not a copy of it with me, but I do not intend to quote from it. The press report dealt with the centralization of housing in the city of Montreal. I would certainly be disturbed if I thought our housing policy were going to have that effect. I feel that facing the possibility of a war, and we cannot say that we are not when we think of the budget that is going to be brought down, if we are going to bring our families together in centralized places we are only going to make them that much more vulnerable to attack. Coming from a rural area as I do, I would say that much consideration should be given to the possibility of allowing lumbering and mining concerns to borrow money to supply the housing needs of their employees.
One of the previous speakers mentioned these shack towns. It is those towns that I am thinking about now. We should encourage better housing in such places. Such mortgages would not cause us concern because these people are working in primary industries. It is in the primary industries that the individual is closest to the payroll. I
[Mr. Leboe.l
say again, let us decentralize our housing and get more development out in the rural areas.
In closing I should like to leave this thought with you. There has been a lot of stress put on the fear of the individual who has a house with a mortgage. If the individual is able to get into the house, his only fear then should be about meeting the payments. I should like to see a provision in the bill that would make it possible for a married man with one child who moved into a small house to be able to enlarge or extend that house at a later date. If the individual happened to have a larger family and be unable to meet the payments, he should be allowed to recapitalize and bring down the payments within his reach. I should like to emphasize the fact that the rural areas have not had proper consideration in connection with housing, and coming from a rural area I can speak authoritatively on that subject.

speechtext:
It is my understanding, Mr. Speaker, that the principle behind this bill is to facilitate the construction of many badly needed homes throughout the Dominion of Canada. Bearing this principle in mind, it is to be hoped that there are no inherent snags in the legislation or any extraneous factors outside the legislation which may in any way frustrate the purpose of the bill. It is my submission that there are such extraneous factors, and also certain inherent snags which may very well frustrate the purpose of the bill.
It is to be hoped if there are many new homes constructed throughout the country as a result of this legislation, those houses which are built, and which I understand are to be under the auspices of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, are different in one respect at least from the houses that have been built in the last few years under the blessing of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Veterans Land Act. The reason I say that is that the houses that have been built have had a monotonous regularity to them. One can go down row upon row of identical houses in these housing developments, identical even to the last daub of paint. I believe these houses will remain a blight on the landscape of our country for many years to come. We shall not get rid of them very easily.
We rather hope that if this legislation is enacted this situation will not occur again. These boxes which go under the name of houses are of such bad design and architecture that no one would really want them except in case of dire necessity or if they were

offered so cheaply that a person would be foolish not to take them. I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members that most of the houses which have been built under the guidance of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the Veterans Land Act are exceedingly expensive. In fact they are far too expensive for people in the low and medium income brackets for whom they are designed.
In addition to that, the designs of these houses, both interior and exterior, leave very much to be desired. There is little doubt but that the reason for the construction of these rows of identical houses has been the result of several factors. Houses of this type allow no room for individuality, which is something most of us look for in this country of ours. This sameness of the houses cannot help but have a levelling down effect on the people who live in them. There is a danger that the new legislation may be frustrated for the following reasons, which are outside the legislation itself. The first of these would be restrictions placed on local building codes. Local building codes have been built up over the years, and are the result of experience. They have been growing up, and they are full of old-fashioned methods and old-fashioned standards. They take into consideration not at all the fact that new types of building materials, new methods of building and new types of architecture, which have been the result of the advancement of modern science, are now available.
As hon. members know, many of these building codes grew up in the thirties, in the depression days. A great many of the restrictions were put in municipal building codes in order to create jobs. These have not been removed and they do not help to improve the housing situation at the present time.
In addition I think it might be safe to say that a great many of these Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation regulations are based on these local building codes, and suffer from some of the same deficiencies. Insufficient attention has been paid to modern advances. The younger people are making attempts to remedy this. I think the present minister should look into the possibility of making arrangements with many of the provincial governments with a view to seeing that these local building codes are altered so that new types of design in housing can be used.
So much for local building codes which may help to frustrate this bill, and so much for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation regulations which, I submit, are not helpful, either. But is it necessary to build
National Housing Act
row upon row of identical houses at a high cost? Is that an excuse for the present situation? We know that people have to have places in which to live, whether they are attractive or unattractive. But I cannot see any reason why buildings should be built in this way. I believe, indeed, that houses could be built at costs lower than the present ones, and in addition to being built at a lower cost they would have several advantages over the present row-on-row boxes. First of all the houses could be individual in style. Then, they could be of better construction and, third, the interior design could be of much greater utility and beauty than the existing houses being constructed today under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
These advantages, in addition to lower costs, could be effected by means of modern design and the use of modern materials which, while apparently the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will not approve, all sorts of private industry and individuals, both here and in other countries, including the United States and the United Kingdom, have been constructing for some years.
I have some information in this regard from Grant Whatmough who, for the information of hon. members, is a young Canadian in his thirties and spent some years in England. He has the following qualifications: He was the chief experimental designer for the British admiralty between 1946 and 1948. He was a member of the council for industrial design in Great Britain in 1948. He was assistant chief consultant to the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario in 1948 and 1949. He has designed over $100 million worth of construction in the United Kingdom, and in the last 19 months in this country designed and supervised the erection of $15 million worth of buildings in the Toronto area. These buildings include the new factory of the International Business Machines Company, as well as those of the Lennox Furnace Company, the Allanson Armature company, and many others.
I think hon. members and the house would agree that Mr. Whatmough's qualifications are very considerable, and that he has obviously some idea of what he is talking about. Mr. Whatmough has designed a number of homes which are very individual and very attractive. They contain four bedrooms, a bathroom, a large living room, a dining room, a utility room and a garage.
These houses, all containing this number of rooms, are of different designs and are not the identical box-like structures one sees

National Housing Act
today. They are the type of design and construction that Mr. Whatmough has utilized in the building of the many factories and other buildings he has designed, and the construction of which he has supervised. These houses can be built for $10,000-that is $8,000 for the house and $2,000 for the land. That price has been laid down by the J. R. Page company which, I understand, is one of the largest contractors in the city of Toronto. The Page company has given a specific contract price on these houses of this design.
Houses of similar area, but of much inferior quality and with a box-like appearance, sell at present for $15,500 to $16,500, and houses of design similar to the ones designed by Mr. Whatmough are of a custom-built nature and cost around $25,000.
I believe it is worth pointing out at this juncture that houses now being built with the approval of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are of such an unattractive design that at the end of five years it has been estimated by many reliable authorities that they would probably sell in the open market for about 20 per cent less than the amount of the mortgage still existing on each house. This can hardly be described as a satisfactory or economic state of affairs.
These suggestions put forward by Mr. Whatmough sound truly incredible; and I understand that a great many of the government agencies and private concerns that have employed him thought his ideas were incredible, too. Those were their thoughts, at least, until they tried them out, and found they were not incredible.
Mr. Whatmough's designs for houses have been examined by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which, I understand, will have to pass upon any plans for homes which will be built under this proposed legislation; and it is to be hoped that those who have the authority of approving such plans will at least consider the possibility of homes of different and new designs, so that new types of construction can be used.
It is my information that in Ontario plans for any houses constructed under the auspices of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have to be approved by one Raymond Card, who is the chief architect for the Ontario division of Central Mortgage and Housing
Corporation. This gentleman has absolute 
authority, which is not appealable, to pass on all designs and plans submitted.
I am informed that Mr. Card came to Canada from England in 1907 and originally set up as an architect. After a brief career in this field he entered the firm of the T. Eaton Company, for which, I am told, he worked as floor manager for some 17 years.* Subsequently Mr. Card became employed by the civil service, and he is now in the position of having the absolute word on the majority of new houses built in Ontario by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
In commenting upon Mr. Whatmough's proposed plans and designs for new homes, Mr. Card indicated that he was not familiar with this type of planning, because it was new to him; and in addition suggested that if houses were too attractive for working people they might develop a taste for an expensive form of living which was not good for them.
It may very well be that Mr. Whatmough's plans and designs for homes to be built at such a low cost are not practicable, although the evidence would indicate that his suggestions were indeed most practicable. But even if they are not, it is a very unfortunate situation that any one person in a large government agency, such as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, is placed in the position of either approving or disapproving absolutely, without any opportunity of appeal by those who are affected.
What we need in this country is attractive, individual, low-cost houses, and we certainly will never get them if this bill is put forward, and is to be frustrated by local building codes and the bureaucracy of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
All through history we have seen examples of people who have followed this line of thinking: "If it was good enough for grandfather, it is good enough for me." In this young and growing country, with the great changes brought about by modern science, I would hope that this attitude might be put aside, at least so far as this bill is concerned. Because we certainly do need more houses, cheap ones and individual ones.
In conclusion, if the government would enter into some arrangement with the provinces to help modernize local building codes, and could alter the regulations under which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation
